name: Once
tagline: A camera app that limits you to a small roll of shots and develops them later, like a disposable camera.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The mechanic is trivial: cap the roll, hide the previews, apply a film-ish grade, unlock the photos on a timer. An agent can produce that as a local app in a session, and the artificial scarcity works exactly as well when you wrote the limit yourself, which is to say it works until you edit your own config. The hard part is not the logic, it is being a good camera: shutter latency, exposure control, and a grade that looks like film instead of an Instagram filter from 2011. Shipping it to your actual phone means Xcode or a signed Android build, which is the real weekend tax. Build it if you want the constraint, not if you want the look.
coreLoopDIY: A camera app that lets you take a fixed number of photos with no live preview, stores them locked, and reveals a graded roll after a set delay.
requirements: A phone and a way to sideload: Xcode with a free Apple ID, or Android Studio
whatYouLose: A film grade someone actually tuned, versus a curve you guessed at
App Store install instead of re-signing a dev build every week
Any social layer or shared rolls with friends
The psychological weight of a limit you cannot quietly raise
Polish: haptics, viewfinder feel, shutter timing, battery behaviour
moatNotes: The entire product is taste: how the grain sits, how the delay feels. That does not show up in a feature list, which is exactly why it is hard to clone.
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay here for taste and for commitment. The grade is the product, and matching it takes more iteration than most people will spend on a hobby build. The delay only functions as a constraint if it is enforced by someone other than you, so a self-hosted version quietly loses the one thing that makes the app work. Cheap enough that the DIY route is a curiosity project, not a savings play.
notes: The logic is an afternoon; the film look is not. Build it to feel the constraint, buy it if you want the photos to look good.
prompt:
Build a local-only disposable camera app for my phone. No backend, no accounts, no telemetry, no cloud upload.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Expo (React Native) with TypeScript, run via Expo Go or a local dev build
- expo-camera for capture, expo-file-system for storage, expo-image-manipulator or a GL shader for grading
- expo-sqlite for the roll metadata
- No analytics library, no auth, no remote API

Core behaviour:
1. A roll has a fixed capacity, default 24 shots, set in a single config file.
2. The capture screen shows a live viewfinder plus only the remaining shot count. No thumbnail of the last photo, no gallery access while a roll is open.
3. Tapping the shutter writes the photo to app-private storage, marked locked, and increments the counter. No review, no retake, no delete.
4. When the roll hits capacity, or when the user taps "finish roll", the roll enters developing state with a reveal timestamp: now plus a configurable delay, default 12 hours.
5. While developing, show only a countdown. Locked photos must not be readable from the UI.
6. At reveal time, apply the film grade once, write the graded JPEGs, and mark the roll viewable.
7. Rolls screen lists past rolls by date with a contact-sheet grid. Tapping an image opens it full screen with a save-to-camera-roll button.

The grade, do this properly:
- Implement as one pass: slight highlight rolloff, lifted blacks with a warm tint, mild saturation boost, per-channel curve, film grain scaled to image size, subtle vignette.
- Put every parameter in grade.ts as named constants with comments so I can tune them.
- Ship three presets: warm, cool, monochrome. Nothing else.

Explicitly out of scope: sharing, friends, feeds, push notifications, in-app purchases, cloud sync, editing after reveal.

Deliverables: working Expo app, README with exact run and device-install steps, and a DEV_UNLOCK flag in config that bypasses the delay for testing. State clearly in the README that the delay is enforced only by local device time and is trivially bypassable.
